name: Go
title: Go from the first line
intro: Go is a small language from Google for programs that stay running: servers, tools and services. It compiles quickly, has a garbage collector, and keeps the grammar short on purpose. These lessons cover printing, names, choices, the one looping keyword, functions and slices. Every example is a whole program and shows exactly what it prints. To run one yourself, save it as hello.go and type go run hello.go.

sections.p: Every file starts with package. A program you can run is package main and has func main. fmt.Println prints its arguments separated by spaces, then a newline. The import path is a string.
fmt.Printf does not add a newline. %d is an integer and %s is a string. \n starts the next line.

practice.why: Println puts a space between arguments and a newline after them. The quotes are not printed.
A line starting with // is a comment and never runs.

practice.q: Which package can you run with go run?
practice.why: main is the package the go command builds into a program. Other names are libraries.

practice.q: What is the difference between Println and Printf?
options: Println adds spaces and a newline; Printf follows the format string
practice.answer: Println adds spaces and a newline; Printf follows the format string
practice.why: Printf prints exactly the format you write, including whether there is a newline.
Each %s is replaced by the next string. The hyphen is an ordinary character.

sections.p: var declares a name. Inside a function, := is a shorter form that both declares and assigns, and Go infers the type. = assigns to a name that already exists.
sections.code:
package main
import "fmt"
func main() {
    nuts := 5
    nuts = nuts + 2
    fmt.Println(nuts)
}

sections.p: A var with no value starts at the zero for its type: 0 for a number, "" for a string, false for a bool. Go does not leave a number uninitialized.

practice.code:
package main
import "fmt"
func main() {
    n := 10
    n = n - 3
    fmt.Println(n)
}
practice.why: := declares n. The next line assigns n - 3 back to it.
A string's zero value is empty, so the brackets have nothing between them.

practice.q: Which line declares a new name and stores 4 in it?
practice.why: := declares and assigns. = only assigns, and it needs a name that already exists.

practice.q: What is the zero value of an int?
practice.why: Numbers start at zero. There is no undefined.

practice.code:
package main
import "fmt"
func main() {
    a := 1
    b := a + 1
    fmt.Println(a, b)
}
practice.why: a stays 1. b is a new name holding a + 1. Println puts a space between them.

sections.p: if does not use brackets around the test. The body is always a block. == compares; = assigns.

practice.why: n == 2 is true, so only the first branch runs.
4 fails the first test and passes the second.
== compares. = assigns. := declares.

practice.q: What surrounds the body of an if?
practice.why: Go always uses braces for the body, even for a single line. There are no brackets around the test.
The test succeeds, so the block runs. There is no else.

lessons.title: The one loop
lessons.summary: for does every kind of repetition.

sections.p: Go has no while and no do. for covers all of them. The three-part form is start, test, step. fmt.Print does not add a newline. continue skips the rest of the current pass.
A for with only a test repeats while the test is true. range walks a collection.

practice.why: i runs through 1, 2 and 3. Print adds no newline, and Println() adds one at the end.
range on a string yields each byte's index and the rune. The index is ignored with _. %c prints the character.

practice.q: How do you write a while loop in Go?
practice.why: for is the only looping keyword. for n > 0 { } is the while shape.

options: Adds 1 to i, as a statement
Returns i + 1 as a value you can embed anywhere
practice.answer: Adds 1 to i, as a statement
practice.why: ++ is a statement in Go, not an expression. You cannot write n = i++.
continue skips the rest of this pass. 2 is not printed.

lessons.title: Functions and slices
lessons.summary: Multiple results, and a slice's length.

sections.p: Parameter types come after the names. The return type comes after the parameter list. A function can return more than one value; the usual second value is an error, ignored here with _.
A slice is a view of a row of values. len is the number of elements. Indexes start at 0. The slice literal []int{10, 20, 30} builds one.

practice.why: twice returns n * 2, called with 4.
Index 0 is the first element. len counts all three.

practice.q: Where is the return type written?
practice.why: func add(a int, b int) int — the final int is what comes back.
Indexes start at 0, so 1 is the second element.
A function with no result type returns nothing. Each call prints one line.

sections.p: A slice is a window onto an underlying array: it has a length (how many elements you can see) and a capacity (how far the array goes). append adds to the end and returns the slice, growing the array when it is full, so always write s = append(s, x). range gives the index and the value of each element; use _ for the one you don't need.
Slicing does not copy. Two slices of the same array see each other's changes, which is fast but can surprise you. copy or slices.Clone makes an independent copy when you need one.

A map stores values by key: map[string]int. Reading a missing key gives the zero value; the two-value form v, ok := m[k] tells you whether it was there. delete removes a key. Go deliberately visits map entries in a random order, so sort the keys when the order matters.
sections.out:
no pine, zero value is 0
hazel 5
oak 12
2 trees

practice.why: t is a window onto the same array as s.
A missing key gives the zero value 0, ok is false, and reading does not add the key.

practice.q: Why write s = append(s, x) rather than just append(s, x)?
options: append may make a new, bigger array and returns the slice that points to it
append only works on maps otherwise
It is only a style rule
practice.answer: append may make a new, bigger array and returns the slice that points to it
practice.why: Discarding the result loses the new element when the array had to grow.

lessons.title: Structs, methods and interfaces
lessons.summary: Your own types, and behaviour they share.

sections.p: A struct groups named fields. Methods are functions with a receiver written before the name. A pointer receiver, (s *Squirrel), lets the method change the value; a value receiver works on a copy. Go has no classes or constructors; a function named NewSomething is the usual way to build a value.

An interface lists methods. Any type that has those methods satisfies the interface automatically; there is no implements keyword. The standard fmt.Stringer interface has one method, String() string, and fmt uses it whenever it prints a value of that type.

A type switch runs different code depending on the concrete type inside an interface value. Embedding one struct in another, by naming only its type, promotes its fields and methods, which is how Go reuses behaviour instead of inheritance.
sections.out:
Pip 3
int 7
string oak
I am Pip
something else

practice.why: The value receiver changes a copy; only the two pointer-receiver calls count.

practice.q: How does a Go type satisfy an interface?
options: By having all the interface's methods; nothing else is needed
By writing implements after the type
By registering it with the interface
practice.answer: By having all the interface's methods; nothing else is needed
practice.why: Go interfaces are satisfied implicitly.

practice.q: What does a String() string method on a type change?
options: How fmt prints values of that type
How the type is stored in memory
practice.answer: How fmt prints values of that type
practice.why: It satisfies fmt.Stringer, which fmt checks for.

sections.p: Go has no exceptions for ordinary failures. A function that can fail returns an error as its last result, and the caller checks it right away: if err != nil. strconv.Atoi, which turns text into an int, works like this. It is more typing, but you can always see where failures are handled.
sections.out:
got 42
error: strconv.Atoi: parsing "forty-two": invalid syntax

sections.p: errors.New makes a simple error, and fmt.Errorf builds one with a message. A %w in fmt.Errorf wraps another error, adding context while keeping the original inside. errors.Is then checks whether a particular error is anywhere in the chain.
sections.out:
6 <nil>
asked for 8, only 3 stored
oak: the store is empty
true

sections.p: defer schedules a call to run when the surrounding function returns, however it returns. It keeps clean-up, such as closing a file, right next to the code that opened it. Deferred calls run in reverse order, last one first.
sections.out:
open store
bury three nuts
count nuts
close store
done

practice.why: Deferred calls run when main returns, last one first.
%w puts the original error's text in the message and keeps it in the chain for errors.Is.

practice.q: How does a Go function usually report failure?
options: By returning an error as its last result
practice.answer: By returning an error as its last result
practice.why: panic is kept for bugs and truly unrecoverable situations.

lessons.title: Goroutines and channels
lessons.summary: Doing several things at once, safely.

sections.p: Writing go f() starts f in a new goroutine, a very lightweight thread; a program can run thousands. Goroutines talk through channels: ch <- v sends a value and v := <-ch receives one, waiting until a value arrives. "Share memory by communicating" is the Go motto.

sync.WaitGroup waits for a group of goroutines to finish. When several goroutines change the same variable, protect it with a sync.Mutex: only the goroutine holding the lock may touch the data. Without it, updates can be lost. go run -race finds such bugs.

A goroutine can read from one channel and write to another, forming a pipeline. close(ch) says no more values are coming, and for v := range ch reads until the channel is closed. A buffered channel, make(chan int, 3), holds a few values so the sender need not wait.

practice.why: The buffer holds both values, and range stops once the closed channel is empty.

practice.q: Why protect a shared counter with a sync.Mutex?
options: Without it, goroutines can overwrite each other's updates
practice.answer: Without it, goroutines can overwrite each other's updates
practice.why: total++ reads, adds and writes; two goroutines doing it at once can lose a count.

options: No more values will be sent
The channel is empty right now
practice.answer: No more values will be sent
practice.why: range over the channel ends after the remaining values are read.

lessons.title: Project: counting words
lessons.summary: Strings, maps, sorting and formatting together.

sections.p: This program counts the words in a short text, ignoring case and punctuation, and prints the most common ones. It splits the text with strings.FieldsFunc, counts in a map, copies the counts into a slice of structs, and sorts that with slices.SortFunc and cmp.Compare: most frequent first, then alphabetically.
sections.out:
21 words, 12 different
the       5
nut       3
a         2
squirrel  2

sections.p: Read the text from a file with os.ReadFile (checking its error), skip stop words such as "a" and "the" with a map[string]bool, or count several files at once, one goroutine each, sending their maps down a channel to be merged.

practice.why: Fields splits on runs of spaces and ignores spaces at the ends.

practice.q: Why copy the map into a slice before printing the top words?
options: Maps have no order, and a slice can be sorted
range does not work on maps
practice.answer: Maps have no order, and a slice can be sorted
practice.why: Go even randomizes map order on purpose so that code does not rely on it.

practice.q: In slices.SortFunc, what should the comparison return when a should come first?
practice.why: cmp.Compare(b.n, a.n) is negative when a has the bigger count, so bigger counts come first.
